newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU's ageing population to radically alter workforce.
newsitem.headline: EU's ageing population to radically alter workforce.

text.p: Europe's workforce will undergo profound changes over the next decade as an ageing population slashes the number of new workers and raises the costs of supporting the elderly, the EU said on Wednesday.

In a report on the demographic outlook for the 15-nation bloc and the countries that have applied to join it, the European Commission predicted that after the year 2010 more people will be leaving the workforce than entering it.
Such a development could ease the current high rate of unemployment in the EU but also raise the costs of caring for a vast number of retired and aged citizens.
"Over the last decades, demographic growth has played a significant role in the labour market by increasing the working age population and expanding the labour supply," the Commission said.
"In the future this will be reversed."

Behind the dire picture is a sharp decline in birth rates since 1970, most noticeable in Italy, and to a lesser extent, in Spain, France and Portugal. This development has resulted in fewer people joining the labour force since 1990.
With no signs of easing in sight, the fall in new workers could last for at least 20 more years and prompt a dramatic demographic change, the Commission added.

Commenting on the report, EU employment and social affairs commissioner Padraig Flynn said the findings showed that "significant changes in the demography of the working age population have to be expected."
The question of how to fund the enormous costs associated with an ageing population has not gone unnoticed by EU governments, many of which face large unfunded pension liabilities.
At a meeting of EU finance ministers this week, Italy was warned that it must further reform its vast pension system in order to cope with the heavy costs arising from an ageing population.

Although the budget consolidation efforts seen across the EU have been largely blamed on the demands of joining a single currency, policy-makers have repeatedly stressed that such reforms would have been necessary even without monetary union.
Even more disturbing, the Commission's report noted that such demographic trends were also seen in central and East European countries, many of whom are eagerly awaiting entry into the EU.
"In half of these countries demographic trends already contribute to increased pressures on social protection systems," the Commission said.
The heavy costs associated with enlargement have been cited as an important factor behind the EU's rather cautious stance in bringing in new members.
The study also found a regional dimension to the problem.
"As the phenomenon of the ageing labour force is felt more acutely at the regional level, regional action is going to be needed."
This last observation could also affect future EU policies on social cohesion, the report said.
